lead: In an ideal gas mixture the molecules ignore each other: no attraction, no reaction, and each gas fills the whole vessel at the mixture temperature. Dalton splits the total pressure into partial pressures p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p; Amagat splits the total volume into partial volumes V<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>V. Both use the mole fraction y<sub>i</sub> as the share. Engineers need this for air, combustion products, LPG–air and natural gas lines, where a compressor or a pipe must be sized for the mixture, not for one gas.
prereq: You need: the ideal gas law pV = nRuT and the kmol from 5.6 Ideal and real gases, plus pressure and the mole concept from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Mole fraction and mixture molar mass

blocks.text: An ideal gas mixture is a set of gases sharing one vessel at the same temperature T and pressure p, with no chemical reaction and no forces between molecules. The amount of each gas is measured in kilomoles: 1 kmol = 1000 mol, and one kmol of gas i has mass M<sub>i</sub> kg, where M<sub>i</sub> is the molar mass in kg/kmol. The total amount is n = n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub> + …, with n<sub>i</sub> the kmol of component i.

The mole fraction of component i is y<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n. It is dimensionless, and Σ y<sub>i</sub> = 1. The mass fraction w<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>i</sub>/m is a different number; for air, y<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.21 but w<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.23. The two are linked by w<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub>/M<sub>mix</sub>.

A mixture behaves as one gas with molar mass M<sub>mix</sub> = m/n = Σ y<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub> and gas constant R<sub>mix</sub> = R<sub>u</sub>/M<sub>mix</sub>, where R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K) is the universal gas constant.

blocks.where: y<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n is the mole fraction, dimensionless; M<sub>i</sub> is the molar mass of component i in kg/kmol; M<sub>mix</sub> is the mixture molar mass in kg/kmol; R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K); R<sub>mix</sub> is the mixture gas constant in kJ/(kg·K).

blocks.text: Dalton's model takes the mixture apart. Put component i alone in the same volume V at the same temperature T. It behaves as an ideal gas and presses on the walls with the partial pressure p<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T/V. Dalton's law states that the mixture pressure is the sum of these partial pressures: p = Σ p<sub>i</sub>.

Divide p<sub>i</sub> by p = nR<sub>u</sub>T/V and the temperature and volume cancel: p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p. The partial pressure is a share of the total, and the share is the mole fraction. Using the mass fraction here is the most common error in this chapter.

items: Convert every amount to kmol, every temperature to K and every volume to m³.
Add: n = Σ n<sub>i</sub>, then y<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n. Check that the y<sub>i</sub> add to 1.00.
Find the mixture pressure: p = nR<sub>u</sub>T/V, with R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K) and p in kPa.
Multiply for each gas: p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p. Check that the p<sub>i</sub> add to p.
For masses use m<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub>, M<sub>mix</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub> and R<sub>mix</sub> = R<sub>u</sub>/M<sub>mix</sub>.

blocks.text: The V and T in step 3 belong to the whole mixture. In the example below, nitrogen and oxygen share one 0.5 m³ tank; nitrogen is not squeezed into a smaller volume of its own. Partial pressure uses the mixture volume and the mixture temperature, always.

Amagat's model keeps the mixture pressure p and temperature T and asks a different question: what volume V<sub>i</sub> would component i occupy alone at p and T? For an ideal gas, V<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T/p = y<sub>i</sub>V. Amagat's law states that the partial volumes add to the vessel volume: V = Σ V<sub>i</sub>.

The same mole fraction appears in both laws: p<sub>i</sub>/p = V<sub>i</sub>/V = y<sub>i</sub>. Dalton and Amagat are two ways of bookkeeping the same ideal-gas model, not two different physical pictures. Use Dalton when a pressure gauge is read. Use Amagat when a gas analyser reports percentages by volume, because for ideal gases volume per cent equals mole per cent.

Mixture properties follow the Gibbs–Dalton rule: u<sub>mix</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>u<sub>i</sub> and h<sub>mix</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>h<sub>i</sub>, each component property taken at the mixture temperature. Entropy of mixing is a finer point, left for later.

Some old notes write Amalgam's law for Amagat's law; the correct name is Amagat. Both laws assume ideal gases. At 200 bar, or near condensation, they fail, and a real mixture needs the compressibility factor or an equation of state with mixing rules (see 5.7 Compressibility factor and chart).

figure.caption: A tank holding 2 kmol of nitrogen and 3 kmol of oxygen: the mole fractions 0.4 and 0.6 split the 24.9 MPa total into 9.98 MPa and 15.0 MPa, so the partial pressures add back to the total.

spec.title: n (kmol), y, p (MPa)
spec.aria: A table lists 2 kilomoles of nitrogen and 3 kilomoles of oxygen, their mole fractions 0.4 and 0.6, and Dalton partial pressures 9.98 and 15.0 megapascals, giving 24.9 megapascals total.

examples.question: A rigid tank of volume 0.5 m³ holds an ideal gas mixture of 2 kmol of nitrogen and 3 kmol of oxygen at 300 K. Take R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K), M<sub>N2</sub> = 28 kg/kmol and M<sub>O2</sub> = 32 kg/kmol. Find the total pressure, the mole fractions, the partial pressure of each gas, the mixture molar mass and the mixture gas constant.
steps: Data: n<sub>N2</sub> = 2 kmol, n<sub>O2</sub> = 3 kmol, V = 0.5 m³, T = 300 K, R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K).
Mole fractions: y<sub>N2</sub> = 2/5 = 0.4 and y<sub>O2</sub> = 3/5 = 0.6; check 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.00.
Partial pressures: p<sub>N2</sub> = 0.4 × 24942 = 9976.8 kPa ≈ 9.98 MPa; p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.6 × 24942 = 14965.2 kPa ≈ 15.0 MPa.
Dalton check: 9976.8 + 14965.2 = 24942 kPa, equal to the total pressure.
Mixture molar mass: M<sub>mix</sub> = 0.4 × 28 + 0.6 × 32 = 11.2 + 19.2 = 30.4 kg/kmol. Mass: m = n M<sub>mix</sub> = 5 × 30.4 = 152 kg.

Mixture gas constant: R<sub>mix</sub> = R<sub>u</sub>/M<sub>mix</sub> = 8.314 / 30.4 = 0.2735 kJ/(kg·K). Check: pV/m = 24942 × 0.5 / 152 = 82.05 kJ/kg and R<sub>mix</sub>T = 0.2735 × 300 = 82.05 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: n = 5 kmol, y<sub>N2</sub> = 0.4, y<sub>O2</sub> = 0.6, p = 24942 kPa (24.9 MPa), p<sub>N2</sub> = 9976.8 kPa (9.98 MPa), p<sub>O2</sub> = 14965.2 kPa (15.0 MPa), M<sub>mix</sub> = 30.4 kg/kmol and R<sub>mix</sub> = 0.2735 kJ/(kg·K).
examples.check:
Ru = 8.314
T = 300.0
V = 0.5
nN2 = 2.0
nO2 = 3.0
n = nN2 + nO2
yN2 = nN2 / n
yO2 = nO2 / n
p = n * Ru * T / V
pN2 = yN2 * p
pO2 = yO2 * p
Mmix = yN2 * 28.0 + yO2 * 32.0
Rmix = Ru / Mmix
print(round(n, 1))
print(round(yN2, 4))
print(round(yO2, 4))
print(round(p, 1))
print(round(pN2, 1))
print(round(pO2, 1))
print(round(Mmix, 1))
print(round(Rmix, 4))

traps: p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p, never p<sub>i</sub> = w<sub>i</sub>p. Air is 0.21 oxygen by mole but 0.23 by mass, so the mass fraction overstates p<sub>O2</sub> by about 10 %.
Partial pressure uses the mixture volume V and the mixture temperature T. Putting a component's own volume into p<sub>i</sub>V = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T is the classic mistake.
R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 works only with kPa, m³, kmol and K. Mixing MPa with m³, or mol with kmol, shifts the answer by a factor of 1000.
The mole fractions must add to 1.00. If an analysis sums to 0.95, a component is missing, not a rounding error.
Amagat's partial volume is not the volume of the gas before mixing. It is the volume that gas would occupy alone at the final p and T.

quiz.q: State Dalton's law of partial pressures and write the formula for the partial pressure of component i.
quiz.a: The total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures, p = Σ p<sub>i</sub>. Each gas alone in the mixture volume V at temperature T gives p<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T/V = y<sub>i</sub>p.

quiz.q: Define mole fraction and mass fraction. Which one appears in Dalton's law?
quiz.a: y<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n and w<sub>i</sub> = m<sub>i</sub>/m, both dimensionless. Dalton uses the mole fraction: p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p.

quiz.q: Why do Dalton's and Amagat's laws give the same mole fractions for an ideal gas mixture?
quiz.a: For an ideal gas pV = nR<sub>u</sub>T holds for the whole mixture and for each component at the same T. So p<sub>i</sub>/p = n<sub>i</sub>/n = V<sub>i</sub>/V = y<sub>i</sub>; the two laws are the same equation rearranged.

quiz.q: A 0.2 m³ tank at 400 K holds 0.5 kmol of CO₂ and 1.5 kmol of N₂. Take R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K). Find the total pressure and the partial pressure of CO₂.
A 4 kg mixture contains 1 kg of O₂ (M = 32 kg/kmol) and 3 kg of N₂ (M = 28 kg/kmol). Find the mole fractions and the mixture molar mass.
A student reports p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.23 bar in air at 1 bar, because oxygen is 23 % by mass. Identify the error and give the correct partial pressure.
quiz.a: 0.23 is a mass fraction. Dalton's law needs the mole fraction y<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21, so p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21 × 1 bar = 0.21 bar. A mass fraction cannot be substituted into p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real gas mixtures at high pressure are handled with cubic equations of state such as van der Waals or Peng–Robinson, plus mixing rules and a binary interaction parameter for each pair of gases. In chemical engineering the same idea returns as the fugacity and chemical potential of each component, which decide how a mixture separates in distillation or absorbs in a scrubber. LNG terminals, natural gas grids and CO₂ capture plants all work with mixtures where Dalton's law is only the first guess. Search next for Kay's rule, pseudo-critical properties and the fugacity coefficient.
